channel.title: AstroAlert – what's happening in space
channel.description: A daily updated guide to astronomical and space events: eclipses, conjunctions, meteor showers, rocket launches, aurorae and close approaches of asteroids.

item.title: Asteroid 2015 HA10 passes by
item.description:
26.09.2026, 21:33 UTC

An asteroid with an estimated diameter of 201–449 m will pass Earth at 38.85 million km, or 101.1 times the Earth–Moon distance, travelling at 15.5 km/s. For scale: roughly the size of a small hill. This is not a close encounter – it makes the list as one of the largest objects passing us this week. The pass is entirely safe – approaches like this happen regularly and are tracked as a matter of routine.

item.title: Orionids meteor shower peak
item.description:
21.10.2027, 02:00 UTC

The year's second helping of dust from Halley's Comet, with fast, bright meteors. At maximum, up to 20 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Orion. Unfortunately the Moon will be 68% illuminated and will drown out the fainter meteors – it is worth observing after it sets. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.

item.title: Draconids meteor shower peak
item.description:
08.10.2027, 02:00 UTC

An unpredictable shower: usually weak, but a few times in history it has produced genuine meteor storms. The radiant is already high in the early evening. At maximum, up to 10 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Draco. A Moon 56% illuminated will brighten the sky a little. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.

item.title: Perseids meteor shower peak
item.description:
12.08.2027, 02:00 UTC

The most popular shower of the year – it falls in the holiday season and on warm nights. Its source is comet 109P/Swift-Tuttle. At maximum, up to 100 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Perseus. Unfortunately the Moon will be 77% illuminated and will drown out the fainter meteors – it is worth observing after it sets. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.
